anchor: Go, for they call you, shepherd
title: Opening: the shepherd
short: Pastoral opening: the poet sends a shepherd to his duties and invites him to return at night to resume 'the quest'.
body: Published in Arnold's Poems (1853), the poem opens in the convention of classical pastoral (Theocritus, Virgil's Eclogues), addressing an unnamed shepherd. The shepherd is told to go and tend his flock by day and come back at evening to 'begin the quest' again, the quest being the search for the Scholar-Gipsy. The shepherd is a pastoral convention rather than a portrait, though Arnold later told his brother that the poem was meant to keep alive memories of walks in the Cumnor hills with Clough and others; his elegy for Clough, 'Thyrsis' (1866), is a companion poem set in the same landscape. The shepherd is addressed only in the first three stanzas, and the speaker continues alone.

title: The ten-line stanza
short: Ten-line stanza rhymed abcbcadeed, with a short sixth line; adapted from the stanza of Keats's odes.
body: Each stanza has ten lines rhyming abcbcadeed: pentameters except the sixth line, a trimeter (here 'But when the fields are still'). The form is widely recognised as a variation on the ten-line stanza Keats used in his great odes of 1819, especially 'Ode to a Nightingale', which also has a short line (its eighth). Arnold's choice links the poem with Keats's mood of longing to escape from the 'fever and the fret' of the world, and the nightingales of stanza 22 (l. 220) make the debt explicit. Arnold used the same stanza, slightly varied, for 'Thyrsis'.

title: wattled cotes; rack; cropp'd herbage
short: Sheepfolds made of woven hurdles; the shepherd's fellows strain ('rack') their throats; grazed grass should not grow a new shoot.
body: A 'cote' is a shelter or pen for animals (as in 'dovecote'), and 'wattled' means made of wattle, stakes interwoven with twigs, the traditional material of sheep hurdles. The shepherd should untie the folds and let the flock out. 'Bawling fellows rack their throats' means his fellow shepherds strain their voices calling him ('rack' as in torture, to stretch). 'Nor the cropp'd herbage shoot another head' means: do not leave the grazed grass time to send up new growth, i.e. graze the flock at once. The diction is deliberately rustic and precise, setting the pastoral scene with real agricultural detail.

title: earthen cruse
short: An earthenware jar or jug for drink; a biblical word.
body: A 'cruse' is a small earthenware pot or jar for liquids. The word was archaic by Arnold's day and chiefly biblical, as in the widow of Zarephath's 'a little oil in a cruse' (1 Kings 17:12). The reaper leaves his coat, basket and drinking jug in a corner of the field, to return at noon. The archaic word lends the harvest scene a timeless, almost scriptural simplicity, preparing for the Scholar-Gipsy's world of 'two hundred years' before.

title: Glanvil's book
short: Joseph Glanvill's The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), source of the story of the poor Oxford scholar who joined the gipsies.
body: Arnold printed a passage from Glanvill as a headnote to the poem. In chapter 20 of The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), the philosopher Joseph Glanvill told of 'a Lad in the University of Oxford' of 'very pregnant and ready parts' who, lacking 'preferment', left for poverty and joined 'a company of Vagabond Gypsies', learning their secret of binding others' thoughts 'by the power of Imagination'. Glanvill used the story to argue that apparently impossible things may be possible. Arnold borrows its phrasing ('pregnant parts', 'preferment's door') and its scene of two old acquaintances meeting the wanderer. The 'two hundred years' of line 131 measures the gap between Glanvill and Arnold. In 1929 Marjorie Hope Nicolson suggested the story's original was the alchemist F. M. van Helmont.

title: arts to rule ... heaven-sent moments
short: The gipsies' art of controlling others' thoughts, which Arnold makes a quasi-spiritual gift dependent on moments of grace.
body: In Glanvill the gipsies 'could do wonders by the power of Imagination', binding others' thoughts; the scholar intends, once he has 'compassed the whole secret', to 'give the world an account' of it. Arnold keeps the plot but changes its emphasis: the secret cannot be learned by method, only in 'heaven-sent moments'. This prepares the poem's central symbol of waiting for 'the spark from heaven' (ll. 120, 171). Critics have read the art as poetic inspiration, as religious faith, or as the integrated mind Arnold felt his age had lost; the poem never says what it finally is.

title: the Hurst; the Berkshire moors
short: Cumnor Hurst, a wooded hill west of Oxford; the 'Berkshire moors' are the uplands of the Cumnor area, then in Berkshire.
body: The Hurst is Cumnor Hurst, a hill about three miles west of Oxford, in the area Arnold and Clough walked as young men. Before the county boundary changes of 1974 the country south and west of the Thames at Oxford lay in Berkshire, hence 'the Berkshire moors' for the higher open ground around Cumnor. The precise local geography is part of the poem's appeal: it is often described as a topographical poem of Oxford's countryside, and many of the places can still be walked.

title: ingle-bench; smock-frock'd boors
short: A bench by the fireside; peasants in the traditional linen smock.
body: An 'ingle' is a fire on a hearth, or the fireside itself (from Scottish Gaelic aingeal, 'fire'), and an ingle-bench is a seat in the chimney-corner. A 'smock-frock' was the loose linen over-garment, often embroidered ('smocked'), worn by English farm labourers. 'Boors' here simply means peasants or rustics (Dutch boer, 'farmer'), not yet with the full modern sense of rudeness. The scene of rustic drinkers coming upon the silent scholar, who then flees, is one of many sightings that build his elusive legend.

title: Cumner hills
short: The Cumnor hills, the low ridge west of Oxford, central to the poem's landscape (Arnold spells 'Cumner').
body: Cumnor is a village on the high ground west of Oxford; the 'Cumner hills' or 'Cumner range' (l. 127) form the skyline seen from the Thames meadows. Arnold's spelling 'Cumner' reflects older usage. The phrase 'green-muffled' captures how the hills look softened by summer foliage. The same hills reappear in 'Thyrsis', where Arnold returns after Clough's death to find the landscape changed. The scholar is imagined haunting their 'shy retreats', places where one may be alone.

title: Bab-lock-hithe; Wychwood
short: A ferry crossing on the upper Thames west of Oxford (now Bablock Hythe); Wychwood is a forest in west Oxfordshire.
body: Bablock Hythe ('hithe' = landing place) is a crossing of the Thames between Cumnor and Stanton Harcourt where a ferry, drawn by a rope, has run for centuries; 'the punt's rope chops round' describes the swing of the ferry-rope in the current. The 'stripling Thames' is the young, narrow upper river. Wychwood, an ancient royal forest north-west of Oxford, gives the 'distant ... bowers' where the scholar picks flowers. The picture of him trailing his fingers in the water with a lap full of flowers recalls pastoral figures and, for some readers, Ophelia.

title: the Fyfield elm in May
short: A great elm at Fyfield, a village south-west of Oxford, where May dances were held.
body: Fyfield is a village about eight miles south-west of Oxford, then in Berkshire. Arnold's maidens dance around its elm on May Day, a traditional English festival of spring; 'Thyrsis' also mentions 'the Fyfield tree'. The flowers the scholar gives them (wood anemone, bluebells, purple orchis) are plants of the local woods and meadows in spring. The maidens can 'report' nothing of what he said, reinforcing his silence and elusiveness.

title: Godstow Bridge; lasher
short: Bridge over the Thames by the ruined Godstow nunnery north of Oxford; a 'lasher' is a weir or the pool below it.
body: Godstow, on the Thames north-west of Oxford beside Port Meadow, has the ruins of a medieval Benedictine nunnery, burial place of Rosamund Clifford, mistress of Henry II. 'Lasher' is a local Thames word for a weir, the water rushing over it, or the pool beneath, a favourite bathing place; 'abandon'd' suggests one no longer in use. The June haymaking, with 'many a scythe in sunshine flames', and the bathers crossing the meadows give a vivid picture of the river's summer life, from which the scholar vanishes.

title: Bagley Wood; Thessaly
short: A wood between Oxford and Abingdon where gipsies camped; 'Thessaly' is a local name, ironically recalling the Greek land of witches.
body: Bagley Wood lies south of Oxford towards Abingdon and was long a camping ground for travellers. The gipsies' tents are 'smoked' and the bushes hung with their washing, 'scarlet patches' and 'shreds of grey'. The 'forest-ground called Thessaly' is evidently a local field- or place-name; the poem's own 'called' marks it as such. Its Greek associations are apt: Thessaly was famous in classical literature as the home of witches and magic (as in Lucan's Pharsalia, book 6, and Apuleius's Metamorphoses), and so suits the gipsies' secret arts.

title: the spark from heaven
short: The central symbol: the inspiration, revelation or grace the scholar awaits, and which the moderns also wait for without hope.
body: The scholar is pictured 'waiting for the spark from heaven to fall', and the phrase returns at line 171 ('Thou waitest for the spark from heaven! and we ...'). It develops the 'heaven-sent moments' of line 50. The spark may be read as poetic inspiration, as religious revelation, as the moment in which the gipsies' secret becomes clear, or more generally as the unifying insight Arnold felt modern life lacked. The image draws on the Promethean fire stolen from heaven and on Pentecostal tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). The scholar waits 'in hope'; the moderns, the poem says, also wait but without hope.

title: Hinksey; Christ-Church hall
short: The winter scene on the causeway toward Hinksey; the lit dining hall of Christ Church, Oxford, seen from the Cumnor ridge.
body: North and South Hinksey are villages just west of Oxford, reached across flood meadows by a raised causeway and wooden bridges, which the speaker imagines crossing in winter. From the 'white brow' of the snow-covered Cumnor ridge the scholar looks back to see the 'line of festal light' in the hall of Christ Church, Oxford's largest college, lit for an evening feast. The image sets the scholar outside the warmth and society of the university he renounced, and the 'sequester'd grange' (secluded farm building) where he sleeps on straw underlines his poverty and solitude.

title: teen
short: Archaic: grief, sorrow, affliction.
body: 'Teen' (Old English tēona, 'injury, harm, grief') was archaic by Arnold's time, surviving in poetic usage from Spenser and Shakespeare (e.g. Miranda's 'the teen that I have turn'd you to', The Tempest 1.2). Paired with 'bliss', it sums up the emotional extremes that 'use' or wear out human nerves. The passage (ll. 141-150) explains why the scholar cannot have died: what kills people is not time but repeated 'shocks' that exhaust their energy, and he has avoided these by devoting himself to one aim.

title: the just-pausing Genius
short: The attendant spirit of each person in Roman belief, here waiting to receive back our exhausted life.
body: In Roman religion a person's genius was the guardian spirit born with him, governing his life and character; Horace calls it 'the companion who rules our natal star' (Epistles 2.2.187-189). Arnold imagines this Genius as 'just-pausing', waiting for the moment when we hand back ('remit') our worn-out life, at which point we are 'what we have been', that is, nothing: dead, or merely part of the past. The classical personification gives a stoic, impersonal account of death, contrasting with the poem's later 'immortal lot' of the scholar.

anchor: Light half-believers of our casual creeds
title: Light half-believers of our casual creeds
short: Arnold's diagnosis of his generation: shallow, uncommitted belief that never issues in action.
body: The moderns are 'half-believers', holding their 'casual creeds' (religious or philosophical) lightly, never deeply feeling or clearly willing, with 'insight' that 'never has borne fruit in deeds'. The passage is one of the best-known statements of Victorian religious doubt, comparable to Arnold's 'Dover Beach' and Clough's poems. The contrast is with the scholar's 'one aim, one business, one desire' (l. 152). Arnold himself wrote to Clough in November 1853 that the poem awakened a 'pleasing melancholy' but did not 'animate' readers, a criticism of exactly this mood.

title: one, who most has suffer'd ... intellectual throne
short: The leading sage of the age, who makes his own suffering his subject; identified variously as Tennyson or Goethe.
body: Among the moderns 'one, who most has suffer'd' becomes the age's chief thinker and 'lays bare' his misery: its 'birth and growth and signs' and the 'anodynes' (pain-killers) that soothe it. Critics have long debated who is meant. A common view identifies Tennyson, whose In Memoriam (1850) chronicled his grief for Arthur Hallam in a long series of lyrics; Isaac Gruber has recently read the poem's medical language as a criticism of In Memoriam. Others suggest Goethe, whom Arnold revered as a sage. The phrase 'This for our wisest!' (l. 191) is sardonic whichever is meant.

title: this strange disease of modern life
short: Arnold's most quoted phrase: modern life as an illness of hurry, divided aims, overtaxed minds and paralysed feelings.
body: The phrase defines the poem's central contrast between the scholar, 'born in days when wits were fresh and clear', and the Victorian present. Its symptoms are listed: 'sick hurry', 'divided aims', 'heads o'ertax'd', 'palsied hearts'. The medical imagery continues in 'infection' and 'feverish contact' (ll. 221-222), so that the scholar must flee as one flees contagion. The diagnosis anticipates Arnold's later prose criticism of his age (Culture and Anarchy, 1869). F. R. Leavis found its charm to be one of relaxation; others see the diagnosis as its lasting strength.

anchor: as Dido did with gesture stern
title: Averse, as Dido did
short: Dido's silent turning away from Aeneas in the underworld (Aeneid 6.450-476).
body: In Virgil's Aeneid, book 6, Aeneas meets the shade of Dido, the Carthaginian queen who killed herself after he abandoned her. He pleads, but she keeps her eyes fixed on the ground, 'turned away' (aversa, 6.469), and flees to the shade of her first husband Sychaeus. Arnold's 'Averse' translates Virgil's word, and 'her false friend' is Aeneas. The scholar should turn from the moderns as Dido turned from her betrayer. The allusion also prepares the Carthaginian (Tyrian) note of the closing simile, since Dido was a Tyrian princess.

title: the nightingales
short: Recalls Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale', the poem of longing to escape the world's fever that underlies Arnold's stanza.
body: The scholar is imagined at night listening 'with enchanted ears, / From the dark dingles' ('dingles' = deep wooded hollows) to the nightingales. The bird, traditionally linked to poetry and to the myth of Philomela, here recalls Keats's ode, in which the speaker wishes to 'fade away' with the bird and forget 'The weariness, the fever, and the fret' of human life. Arnold's 'feverish contact' in the very next line echoes that 'fever'. The scholar has already achieved what Keats's speaker only longed for.

title: the Tyrian trader simile
short: Closing epic simile: a Phoenician merchant, seeing Greek traders invade his waters, sails west to trade with the Iberians; its application is disputed.
body: The poem ends with an extended Homeric simile. A 'grave' Tyrian (Phoenician) trader sees a 'merry Grecian coaster' arriving among the Aegean isles with luxury goods, recognises 'the intruders on his ancient home', and sails the length of the Mediterranean to trade with the 'dark Iberians' of Spain. The scholar's flight from moderns is thus compared to the older, graver civilisation withdrawing before a lighter, newer one. Critics disagree about the fit: the scholar, not the moderns, seems the old trader, yet the 'light-hearted' Greeks hardly resemble the 'feverish' Victorians. Isaac Gruber has proposed a link with Tennyson; others read the simile as an image of the poet's own withdrawal into art.

title: Grecian coaster; Chian wine; tunnies
short: The Greek ship's cargo: grapes, wine of Chios (prized in antiquity), figs and tuna in brine.
body: A 'coaster' is a vessel that trades along coasts. Chios, an Aegean island off Asia Minor, produced one of the most famous wines of the ancient world. 'Tunnies' are tuna, salted or pickled in brine, a staple trade item of the Greek world. The rich sensuous list of goods characterises the Greeks as 'young light-hearted masters of the waves', in contrast to the 'grave' Tyrian. Historically the Phoenicians had been the dominant seafarers of the Mediterranean before Greek colonisation spread from the eighth century BC.

anchor: Betwixt the Syrtes and soft Sicily
title: Midland waters; Syrtes; western straits; Iberians
short: The trader crosses the Mediterranean, passes the dangerous Syrtes off Libya, and through Gibraltar trades with the Iberians.
body: 'Midland waters' translates the Latin mare mediterraneum, the sea 'in the middle of the land'. The Syrtes are two shallow, treacherous gulfs on the North African coast (modern Libya and Tunisia), feared by ancient sailors; Acts 27:17 refers to fears of running onto these 'quicksands'. The 'western straits' are the Strait of Gibraltar, beyond which the Atlantic 'raves'. The 'shy traffickers, the dark Iberians' and the merchant who 'undid his corded bales' on the beach recall Herodotus's account (4.196) of the Carthaginians' 'silent trade' beyond the Pillars of Heracles, where goods were laid on the shore and exchanged without speech. The silent trade suits the scholar's silence.
